programs.title: Hello, TI-74
programs.summary: Your first program: display a message and keep it on the screen.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Read the message; press ENTER to end the pause.
notes: Line 10 is a comment; it produces no output.
Line 20 combines PRINT and PAUSE on one line, separated by a colon.
PAUSE lets you read the output before continuing.
programs.experiment: Change the text in quotation marks. Use up to 31 characters to fit the display.
programs.code:
10 REM FIRST PROGRAM
20 PRINT "HELLO, TI-74!":PAUSE
30 END

programs.title: Expressions and order of operations
programs.summary: Compare operations with and without parentheses, and combine powers with square roots.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER between the two screens and again at the end.
programs.expected: First: A=14 and B=20. Then: C=41.
notes: Line 20 uses LET; later assignments omit this optional keyword.
A multiplies before adding. B uses parentheses to add first.
C combines 2 to the fifth power with the square root of 81.
programs.experiment: Replace 2^5 with 2^8 and predict the new value of C before running.
programs.code:
10 REM EXPRESSIONS
20 LET A=2+3*4
30 B=(2+3)*4
40 C=2^5+SQR(81)
50 PRINT "A=";A;" B=";B:PAUSE
60 PRINT "C=";C:PAUSE
70 END

programs.title: Add the numbers from 1 to 10
programs.summary: A counter and an accumulator demonstrate the structure of a loop.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. The total stays visible until you press ENTER.
notes: Line 20 initializes S before the loop.
Lines 30–50 step through I from 1 to 10 and add each value to S.
After the program ends, type S and press ENTER to inspect the variable.
programs.experiment: Change the upper limit to 100. The total should become 5,050.
programs.code:
10 REM ACCUMULATOR
20 S=0
30 FOR I=1 TO 10
40 S=S+I
50 NEXT I
60 PRINT "SUM=";S:PAUSE
70 END

programs.title: Countdown
programs.summary: A negative step runs a loop in reverse order.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to step through 3, 2, 1, and GO.
notes: Line 20 uses STEP -1 to decrease the counter.
The pause is inside the loop: each number waits for ENTER.
programs.experiment: Start at 10 and use STEP -2. Which values appear?
programs.code:
10 REM REVERSE LOOP
20 FOR I=3 TO 1 STEP -1
30 PRINT I:PAUSE
40 NEXT I
50 PRINT "GO":PAUSE
60 END

programs.title: Temperature converter
programs.summary: Ask the user for a value and convert it to another unit.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. At CELSIUS?, type 25 and press ENTER. Press ENTER again to close the result.
notes: Line 20 displays a prompt and stores the answer in C.
Line 30 applies F=C×9/5+32; use a period as the decimal separator.
programs.experiment: Convert in the other direction: ask for F and calculate (F-32)*5/9.
programs.code:
10 REM CELSIUS TO FAHRENHEIT
20 INPUT "CELSIUS? ";C
30 F=C*9/5+32
40 PRINT "F=";F:PAUSE
50 END

programs.title: Validate and decide: odd or even
programs.summary: Validate an integer and choose one of two responses.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Enter an integer from 0 to 100. Also try -1 or 2.5; press ENTER after the error message to try again.
programs.expected: 7 → ODD; 8 → EVEN. Invalid values display INTEGER FROM 0 TO 100.
notes: Line 30 rejects negatives, values above 100, and numbers with a fractional part.
Line 40 compares N with twice the integer part of N/2.
GOTO 20 returns to the prompt after invalid input.
programs.experiment: Change the test to identify multiples of 3.
programs.code:
10 REM VALIDATE AN INTEGER
20 INPUT "NUMBER 0 TO 100? ";N
30 IF N<0 OR N>100 OR N<>INT(N) THEN 80
40 IF N=2*INT(N/2) THEN PRINT "EVEN" ELSE PRINT "ODD"
50 PAUSE
60 GOTO 100
80 PRINT "INTEGER FROM 0 TO 100":PAUSE
90 GOTO 20
100 END

programs.title: Slice, join, and search text
programs.summary: Explore the string operations available in this BASIC dialect.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to advance between the two results.
programs.expected: BASIC / ALC; then LEN=8 and POS=5.
notes: A$ and B$ are string variables.
Line 30 builds B$ from two parts of A$ using the & operator.
Line 50 measures the text and searches for CAL starting at position 1.
programs.experiment: Change BASICALC to CALCULATOR and adjust the slices.
programs.code:
10 REM STRING OPERATIONS
20 A$="BASICALC"
30 B$=SEG$(A$,1,5)&" / "&SEG$(A$,6,3)
40 PRINT B$:PAUSE
50 PRINT "LEN=";LEN(A$);" POS=";POS(A$,"CAL",1):PAUSE
60 END

programs.title: Text, character codes, and numbers
programs.summary: Convert characters to codes and numeric strings to values.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to see each result.
notes: ASC converts A to its character code; CHR$ converts the next code to B.
VAL converts 12.5 from text to a number before multiplication.
STR$ lets you join a numeric result to a message.
programs.experiment: Replace A with Z and see which character comes next.
programs.code:
10 REM CONVERSIONS
20 A=ASC("A")
30 B$=CHR$(A+1)
40 N=VAL("12.5")*2
50 PRINT "ASCII=";A:PAUSE
60 PRINT "LETTER=";B$:PAUSE
70 PRINT "DOUBLE="&STR$(N):PAUSE
80 END

programs.title: Read and reread a data table
programs.summary: Store a small table in the program and restart reading it.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to advance from the total to the first item read again.
notes: Line 20 contains four values; READ consumes one at a time.
RESTORE 20 returns to the beginning of the table.
DATA is on its own line.
programs.experiment: Change the four values and check the new total.
programs.code:
10 REM DATA TABLE
20 DATA 4,7,9,10
30 S=0
40 FOR I=1 TO 4
50 READ X
60 S=S+X
70 NEXT I
80 PRINT "TOTAL=";S:PAUSE
90 RESTORE 20
100 READ X
110 PRINT "FIRST=";X:PAUSE
120 END

programs.title: Mean and standard deviation
programs.summary: Store observations in an array and calculate descriptive statistics in two passes.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to advance from the mean to the population standard deviation.
notes: Line 20 allocates A(0) through A(8); this example uses indices 1 through 8.
Lines 100–120 accumulate squared differences from the mean.
Line 130 divides by 8 to calculate the population standard deviation.
programs.experiment: For the sample standard deviation of the same data, divide by 7 before applying SQR.
programs.code:
10 REM POPULATION STATISTICS
20 DIM A(8)
30 DATA 2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9
40 S=0
50 FOR I=1 TO 8
60 READ A(I)
70 S=S+A(I)
80 NEXT I
90 M=S/8:V=0
100 FOR I=1 TO 8
110 V=V+(A(I)-M)^2
120 NEXT I
130 D=SQR(V/8)
140 PRINT "MEAN=";M:PAUSE
150 PRINT "STDDEV=";D:PAUSE
160 END

programs.title: A 2 × 2 matrix
programs.summary: Use two indices and nested loops to calculate a determinant.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to close the determinant result.
notes: Line 20 allocates a matrix; indices 1 and 2 are used in each dimension.
Lines 40–80 fill one row at a time.
Line 90 subtracts the product of the secondary diagonal from the product of the main diagonal.
programs.experiment: Use the data 1,0,0,1: the identity matrix has determinant 1.
programs.code:
10 REM 2 BY 2 DETERMINANT
20 DIM A(2,2)
30 DATA 1,2,3,4
40 FOR I=1 TO 2
50 FOR J=1 TO 2
60 READ A(I,J)
70 NEXT J
80 NEXT I
90 D=A(1,1)*A(2,2)-A(1,2)*A(2,1)
100 PRINT "DET=";D:PAUSE
110 END

programs.title: Reuse a subroutine
programs.summary: Calculate two hypotenuses using the same block of code.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to advance from the first hypotenuse to the second.
notes: GOSUB 200 calls the subroutine, and RETURN goes back to the next statement.
A, B, and H are shared with the main program.
GOTO 900 prevents execution from falling through into the subroutine again.
programs.experiment: Change the second pair to 8 and 15. The hypotenuse will be 17.
programs.code:
10 REM REUSABLE HYPOTENUSE
20 A=3:B=4:GOSUB 200
30 PRINT "H1=";H:PAUSE
40 A=5:B=12:GOSUB 200
50 PRINT "H2=";H:PAUSE
60 GOTO 900
200 H=SQR(A^2+B^2)
210 RETURN
900 END

programs.title: A subprogram with parameters
programs.summary: Put an operation in a named subprogram with arguments.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Read the result and press ENTER.
notes: Line 30 passes A and B to the DOUBLE subprogram.
Lines 100–120 use X and Y as parameters; assigning to Y returns the result in B.
The subprogram appears after the END of the main program.
programs.experiment: Call DOUBLE again, using B as input and another variable as output.
programs.code:
10 REM SUBPROGRAM WITH PARAMETERS
20 A=7:B=0
30 CALL DOUBLE(A,B)
40 PRINT "DOUBLE=";B:PAUSE
50 END
100 SUB DOUBLE(X,Y)
110 Y=2*X
120 SUBEND

programs.title: Angles and logarithms
programs.summary: Compare degrees with radians and check inverse functions.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to advance through the three screens. The program restores DEG before finishing.
notes: DEG and RAD explicitly set the angle unit before calculating SIN.
PI/6 radians equals 30 degrees.
LOG(1000) uses base 10; LN reverses EXP.
programs.experiment: Compare SIN(90) in DEG mode with SIN(PI/2) in RAD mode.
programs.code:
10 REM SCIENTIFIC FUNCTIONS
20 DEG
30 A=SIN(30)
40 RAD
50 B=SIN(PI/6)
60 C=LOG(1000):D=LN(EXP(2))
70 DEG
80 PRINT "DEGREES=";A:PAUSE
90 PRINT "RADIANS=";B:PAUSE
100 PRINT "LOG=";C;" LNEXP=";D:PAUSE
110 END

programs.title: Format numbers
programs.summary: Control decimal places with a format stored in an IMAGE line.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to advance from 12.50 to 3.14.
notes: Line 100 defines the format on its own line.
PRINT USING reuses the same format for two numbers.
The format changes the display without changing the value stored in A.
programs.experiment: Replace ###.## with ###.### and observe the zeros and rounding.
programs.code:
10 REM TWO DECIMAL PLACES
20 A=12.5
30 PRINT USING 100,A:PAUSE
40 A=PI
50 PRINT USING 100,A:PAUSE
60 GOTO 200
100 IMAGE "###.##"
200 END

programs.title: Roll two dice
programs.summary: Turn pseudorandom numbers into integers from 1 to 6.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. View the two dice, then press ENTER to see their sum.
programs.expected: Each die is in the range 1–6; their sum is in the range 2–12. The seed 74 makes the experiment repeatable.
notes: Line 20 sets the seed to make the demonstration reproducible.
INT(6*RND)+1 turns a fraction into a die roll.
RND is used without parentheses.
programs.experiment: Change the seed. For a 20-sided die, replace 6 with 20.
programs.code:
10 REM TWO DICE
20 RANDOMIZE 74
30 A=INT(6*RND)+1
40 B=INT(6*RND)+1
50 S=A+B
60 PRINT "DICE=";A;B:PAUSE
70 PRINT "SUM=";S:PAUSE
80 END

programs.title: Sort five values
programs.summary: A bubble sort combines arrays, loops, and decisions.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Press ENTER to step through the five sorted values.
notes: Lines 40–60 load the data into the array.
Lines 70–110 compare neighbors and use T as a temporary variable when swapping.
The limit 5-I reduces the work on each pass.
programs.experiment: Replace > with < on line 90 to sort in descending order.
programs.code:
10 REM BUBBLE SORT
20 DIM A(5)
30 DATA 9,2,7,1,4
40 FOR I=1 TO 5
50 READ A(I)
60 NEXT I
70 FOR I=1 TO 4
80 FOR J=1 TO 5-I
90 IF A(J)>A(J+1) THEN T=A(J):A(J)=A(J+1):A(J+1)=T
100 NEXT J
110 NEXT I
120 FOR I=1 TO 5
130 PRINT A(I):PAUSE
140 NEXT I
150 END

programs.title: Position text on the LCD
programs.summary: Build a text bar and write starting at a chosen column.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Read the title and bar; press ENTER to advance to the message at column 8.
programs.expected: TI-74 followed by eight asterisks; then COLUMN 8 starts at the eighth position.
notes: Line 20 clears the line; the semicolon keeps its contents for the next write.
Line 30 places the bar starting at column 10.
RPT$ creates eight asterisks without typing each one.
programs.experiment: Replace 8 with 15 in RPT$ and move the bar using AT.

programs.title: Read a key without ENTER
programs.summary: Show a character as soon as it is typed, along with its character code.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. At PRESS A LETTER, press A without ENTER. Then use ENTER to advance through the results.
programs.expected: KEY=A and CODE=65 for uppercase A; lowercase a has code 97.
notes: Line 30 waits for a keyboard character.
The response does not require ENTER.
The code depends on the letter and the uppercase setting of the TI-74.
programs.experiment: Try a digit or a punctuation mark.
programs.code:
10 REM SINGLE KEY INPUT
20 PRINT "PRESS A LETTER"
30 A$=KEY$
40 PRINT "KEY=";A$:PAUSE
50 PRINT "CODE=";ASC(A$):PAUSE
60 END

programs.title: Approximate a square root
programs.summary: Implement Newton’s method and compare the result with SQR.
programs.instructions: Press RUN and ENTER. Enter 2; press ENTER to advance from the approximation to SQR(2). Values must be greater than 0 and no greater than 1,000,000. Enter numbers without thousands separators.
programs.expected: With 2: about 1.414213562 on both screens. With 81: 9.
notes: Lines 20–30 validate the range used in this demonstration.
Line 60 calculates a new approximation from the previous one.
Lines 70–90 repeat until the difference is small or 40 iterations have been reached.
programs.experiment: Change the tolerance 1E-9 and inspect I after the program to compare the iteration count.
programs.code:
10 REM NEWTON SQUARE ROOT
20 INPUT "POSITIVE NUMBER? ";N
30 IF N<=0 OR N>1000000 THEN 20
40 X=N:I=0
50 P=X
60 X=(X+N/X)/2
70 I=I+1
80 IF ABS(X-P)<1E-9 THEN 110
90 IF I<40 THEN 50
110 PRINT "NEWTON=";X:PAUSE
120 PRINT "SQR=";SQR(N):PAUSE
130 END
